query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing conventional EAM reference potentials with a machine‐learned interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on ab initio MD data sampled across many representative liquid and high‐temperature solid configurations will improve the phase‐space overlap between the reference and target systems in thermodynamic integration of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (including refractory HEAs) in both their solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an MLIP (e.g., using neural network or Gaussian approximation potential frameworks) that is trained on a diverse set of ab initio configurations representative of the wide atomic configurations in the liquid and near-melting phases, then use this MLIP as the reference in the TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration scheme.
generation.conditions: Applicable for alloys with five or more elements, especially those with high melting temperatures (within approximately ±50 K of the melting point), where the liquid and high-temperature solid states exhibit a broad configuration space.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLIP’s ability to accurately emulate the ab initio energy landscape over a wide range of local atomic environments mediates the enhancement in phase-space sampling compared to the more limited EAM functional form.
generation.mechanism: By being trained on ab initio data from a large ensemble of local configurations, the MLIP better captures the complex interatomic interactions and statistical fluctuations present in the ab initio liquid. This results in improved phase-space overlap and a reduced mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in thermodynamic integration path mismatch—on the order of approximately 25-30% improvement relative to TOR-TILD’s original EAM references—yielding free energy estimates that are in closer agreement with direct ab initio predictions.
generation.baseline: The standard TOR-TILD approach using conventional EAM potentials as the reference for thermodynamic integration.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected only when the MLIP is sufficiently trained on an adequately diverse ab initio dataset so that nearly all relevant configurations at high temperature are sampled. In cases where the training set is incomplete or for alloys with extreme compositional or configurational complexity, the improvement may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the reduction in integration path mismatch is uncertain and may depend on the quality and breadth of the ab initio training data as well as the specific alloy composition and temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Select one or several multicomponent high-entropy alloys with well-characterized high melting behavior. First, generate an extensive ab initio MD dataset covering both the liquid state and high-temperature solid state. Develop an MLIP based on this dataset. Then perform thermodynamic integration using the TOR-TILD method twice: once with the standard EAM reference and once with the new MLIP. Compare the integration path discrepancies by analyzing the phase-space overlap metrics and free energy differences relative to a direct ab initio free-energy calculation.
measurements: Quantitative phase-space overlap metrics between the reference and ab initio configurations.
Thermodynamic integration path mismatch (e.g., cumulative free-energy differences along the integration path).
Direct comparison of free energies computed via ab initio MD vs. TOR-TILD using both potentials.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP does not achieve at least a ~20-25% reduction in the thermodynamic integration path mismatch compared to the EAM reference (or if the free energy estimates do not converge significantly closer to the ab initio benchmark), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.
